## Repeated sampling

repeatedly draw random samples of the same size from a population. compute the mean for each sample --> distribution of sample means converges to a normal distribution 

We simulate this on a computer 

Basic idea of simulations is to generate repeated samples under a process you design --> check things are working the way they are supposed to 

* define a data generating mechanism (eg. normal distribution)
* draw a random sample from that data generating mechanism 
* analyze the sample (eg. compute sample mean)
* repeat 
* understand the analysis approach under repeated sampling 

Simulations are natural in the context of iteration 

write a function to

* define data generating mechanism 
* draw a sample 
* analyze the sample 
* return object of interest
* use a loop to analyze this many times 

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1)
```

# Mean and SD 

Can we check central limit theorem using simulations 

```{r}
sim_mean_sd(n_obs = 30)
```

```{r}
output = vector("list", length = 1000)

for (i in 1:1000) {
  
  output[[i]] = sim_mean_sd(n_obs = 30, mu = 12, sigma = 3)
}
```
 inspect results 
 
```{r}
output |> 
  bind_rows() |> 
  summarize(
    emp_m = mean(mean), #empirical mean - taking average across all 1000 numbers in mean column
    emp_se = sd(mean) #empirical standard error - sd of means in mean column 
  )
```
 
```{r}
output |> 
  bind_rows() |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = mean)) +
  geom_density() #starts to approximate normal distribution 
```
 
can edit sim_mean_sd.R doc --> x = rbinom(n = n_obs, size = 1, prob = .5) 

Move output list into a df - use tibbles and map instead

```{r}
sim_results_df = 
  tibble(
    samp_size = rep(30, 1000) #sample size is repeat 30 1000 times
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    est_df = map(samp_size, sim_mean_sd) #add a column, map across samp size column, applying function every time - makes dataframe of df 
  ) |> 
  unnest(est_df) #unnest so it shows in df 
```

look at results 

```{r}
sim_results_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = mean)) +
  geom_density()
```

# Change `n`

narrower sample sizes = narrower sample distributions 

```{r}
sim_results_df = 
  expand_grid( #create a df that has all possible combos of these two inputs
    samp_size = 30, 
    iter = 1:1000
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    est_df = map(samp_size, sim_mean_sd)
  ) |> 
  unnest(est_df)
```

```{r} 
sim_results_df = # {r cache = TRUE} doesn't re run every time you knit, just saves result once. helpful if going slowly
  expand_grid(
    samp_size = c(30, 60, 120, 240), #making more options for combos, running same thing a bunch of times
    iter = 1:1000
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    est_df = map(samp_size, sim_mean_sd)
  ) |> 
  unnest(est_df)
```

```{r}
sim_results_df |> 
  mutate(
    samp_size = str_c("n = ", samp_size), 
    samp_size = fct_inorder(samp_size)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = samp_size, y = mean)) +
  geom_violin()
```

Look at the numbers 

```{r}
sim_results_df |> 
  mutate(
    samp_size = str_c("n = ", samp_size), 
    samp_size = fct_inorder(samp_size)
  ) |> 
  group_by(samp_size) |> 
  summarize(
    emp_m = mean(mean), 
    emp_se = sd(mean)
  )
```

# SLR!! Regression 

Generate once
```{r}
sim_data = 
  tibble(
    x = rnorm(30, mean = 1, sd = 1), 
    y = 2 + 3 * x + rnorm(30, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  )

#sim_data |> 
 # ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y)) +
 # geom_point() +
 # geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

fit = lm(y ~ x, data = sim_data)
```

Write a function that generates the data, gives me the outputs I care about. then do it a bunch of times.

Function is now in source file - use to run over and over 

this works once: 

```{r}
sim_slr(30)
```

this works a lot of times:

```{r}
slr_results_df = 
  tibble(
    samp_size = rep(30, 1000)
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    est_df = map(samp_size, sim_slr)
  ) |> 
  unnest(est_df)
```

is this right?

```{r}
slr_results_df |> 
  summarize(
    b0_mean = mean(beta0_hat), 
    b0_se = sd(beta0_hat)
  )
```

look at results 

```{r}
slr_results_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = beta0_hat)) +
  geom_density()
```
Check it is normally distributed - sometimes samp size won't be big enough to be normally distributed 

```{r}
slr_results_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = beta0_hat, y = beta1_hat)) +
  geom_point()
```
they're correlated!
